Kentucky's plan (KY OSH) adopts the federal excavation rule, so trench protection is required from 5 ft (803 KAR 2:415, adopting 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P) [1].
- Kentucky also lists state-specific standards, such as fall protection for residential construction, steel erection and cranes.
- Whether those fall protection rules still apply after the 2025 law is not confirmed; ask Kentucky OSH.
- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: Kentucky's other state-specific standards and the reporting rule?
q: What construction rules are specific to this state?

text:
Under federal OSHA, which covers Oklahoma private crews, the competent person must inspect and fix hazards, using these steps (1926.651(k)):
1. Inspect the excavation, adjacent areas and protective systems before work starts.
2. Inspect again as needed through the shift and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing event.
3. Remove exposed workers if you find cave-in signs, protective system failure or a hazardous atmosphere.
4. Decide what protection the trench gets; a system is required at 5 ft or deeper (1926.652(a)(1)).
5. Monitor water removal equipment and inspect after heavy runoff (1926.651(h)).
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: What does the competent person have to do on an excavation?

text:
In Indiana, call at least two full working days before you dig, but no more than ten calendar days ahead (Ind. Code 8-1-26) [1].
- Work can start 7 a.m. the next working day after those two days, or sooner if every operator has posted a positive response.
- The statute copy says ten days for the earliest call, but the Indiana 811 FAQ says 20; not confirmed, so ask Indiana 811.
q: How many days before we dig do I have to call 811?

A shoulder taper is at least one third of the merging taper length L (MUTCD Table 6B-3), using the shoulder width as W.
- L = W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less, and L = W x S at 45 mph or more; an 8 ft shoulder at 45 mph is 120 ft.
- Kansas uses the national MUTCD formulas; the approved traffic control plan or permit governs.
- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: taper lengths by speed for other shoulder widths?
q: How long is a shoulder taper?

Hawaii's exact tolerance-zone distance is not confirmed. HRS 269E-12 to 269E-14 were not read, so check with the Hawaii One Call Center (811) or your ticket before running the machine near the marks.
- Marks show approximate location, not depth, so hand-dig or vacuum-expose the line inside the zone first.
- OSHA requires finding the exact location of lines when excavation approaches them (29 CFR 1926.651(b)(3)).
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: How close to the locate marks can I dig with the excavator?

text:
OSHA requires a protective system at 5 feet or deeper, unless the excavation is entirely in stable rock (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)) [3][7].
- Under 5 ft still needs one if the ground shows any sign of cave-in.
- Depth counts at each point where it is 5 ft or deeper, not an average.
- This is the federal rule; the library has no Iowa rule, so confirm with Iowa's OSHA plan.
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: What depth needs trench protection?

text:
OSHA requires that no one work in a trench with accumulated or accumulating water unless adequate precautions are taken against the water hazard (29 CFR 1926.651(h)(1)).
- Precautions can include a shield or support system, water removal, or a harness and lifeline.
- If pumps control the water, a competent person must monitor the pumping (1926.651(h)(2)).
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: There is water in the bottom of the trench. Can we work in it?

text:
No: OSHA requires protection at each point where the trench is 5 feet or deeper, and an average depth can't be used (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)); Georgia follows federal OSHA for private crews.
- The 6 ft tie-in needs a box, shoring, or a slope; the 4 ft stretches need it only if signs of a cave-in show.
- OSHA's 2004 letter says a short deep spot still counts, because an excavation has no minimum length.
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: Most of my trench is 4 ft but one spot is 6 ft at the tie-in. Can I go by the average depth?

text:
The MUTCD (Section 6N.01) calls traffic-control work long-term stationary when it stays in one spot more than 3 days. OSHA's trench rules (Subpart P) have no "long-term stationary" category.

- Intermediate-term is more than one daylight period up to 3 days, or night work over 1 hour.
- Long-term zones run into the night, so devices must be retroreflective or illuminated.
- Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan govern the job.
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: When is a job long-term stationary?

text:
Iowa DOT requires cover of the pipe's nominal diameter or 3 feet, whichever is greater, over a roadway culvert that construction traffic will cross (Section 2417.03.B).

- This applies to corrugated metal or polyethylene culverts; normal roadway culvert cover is 2 feet.
- City street work in Iowa usually follows SUDAS instead, so check the job's specs.
q: How much cover over a roadway culvert if construction traffic will cross it?

text:
The library has no confirmed INDOT deflection limit for plastic pipe. It is not confirmed, so check the base Section 715 and Section 211 text or ask the INDOT Engineer.

- INDOT Section 715 (RSP 715-R-809) mandrel tests plastic pipe, with at least 10 percent of each material's length tested.
- Indiana's number is not stated. Ten States Standards and many agencies use 5 percent, but that is not INDOT's confirmed figure.
q: What is the INDOT deflection limit for plastic pipe?

text:
OSHA requires a protective system (trench box, shoring, sloping or benching) in any trench 5 feet or deeper (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)), and Texas follows federal OSHA for private crews.
- The only exception at 5 ft or deeper is an excavation entirely in stable rock.
- Under 5 ft still needs protection if the ground shows any sign of a cave-in.
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: At what depth does a trench need a trench box or shoring?

text:
MOSH is Maryland's own OSHA plan, and it has state-specific rules in COMAR 09.12 (injury records, steel erection fall protection, cranes, tower crane operator certification, tree care, heat stress, hazard communication, field sanitation, crane personnel platforms) [1].
- Heat stress (COMAR 09.12.32) applies at a heat index of 80 F or more: water, shade, a written heat plan and training [2].
- MOSH also supplements the federal excavation, confined space, lead and crane rules; what they add is not confirmed, so read the MOSH text or ask MOSH [1].
- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: the heat stress rest-break requirements?
q: What rules are specific to MOSH?

No: a head strike from a bucket should be treated as a possible concussion, so he should not go back to work or drive that day, and he should be seen by a doctor with someone staying with him [6].
- Any danger sign (worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, unequal pupils) means call 911 [6].
- Tell your foreman or superintendent now; they decide on OSHA recording and reporting [8].
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: Laborer got hit in the head by the bucket and says he is fine. Can he go back to work?

text:
No, OSHA says stacked shields don't all have to be designed for the deepest part of the trench; each box only has to be used at a depth not greater than it is designed for (OSHA letter, Oct 29, 1991; 29 CFR 1926.652(c)(2)).
- Stack only as the manufacturer's tabulated data allows, with the deeper-rated box on the bottom.
- Keep the data sheet on site, and pin the boxes together as it directs.
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: Does the top trench box in a stack need to be rated for the whole depth?

text:
OSHA allows alternate procedures only when all physical hazards are eliminated or isolated, the only hazard is atmospheric, and continuous forced-air ventilation alone keeps the space safe (29 CFR 1926.1203(e)).
- Needs documented monitoring data, air tested before entry, continuous monitoring, and a signed certification at the entrance.
- Any engulfment, machinery, electrical or surging-flow hazard means a full permit.
- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: the full ventilation, testing and certification steps?
q: When can we use alternate procedures instead of a full permit?

text:
Pennsylvania's own plate rule isn't in the excerpts. The plate has to be thick enough for the trench width and highway loading, and the agency's permit table sets the exact size (not confirmed here; ask the Philadelphia Streets Department or PennDOT permit office).

- For reference, Caltrans uses 1 inch A-36 steel for a trench up to 3 ft 5 in wide.
- Plates need at least 12 inches of bearing, pinned or anchored, with ramped edges.
- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: Caltrans thickness by trench width?
q: How strong does a cover over a hole in the road have to be?

text:
No, not under Table 1 if the operator works from an enclosed cab (29 CFR 1926.1153(c), row xvii): hoe-ramming shows no respirator required for either ≤4 or >4 hours/shift.

- The cab must be a proper enclosed cab (sealed, filtered, positive pressure), and workers outside it need water or dust suppressants.
- If the cab controls aren't fully implemented, a respirator may still be required (1926.1153(e)).
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: Does running a hoe ram on rock need a respirator for the operator?

text:
Stand ahead of the work space, far enough back that a driver who runs the stop can still stop, where approaching drivers see you early (MUTCD 6D.06).
- Distance is the stopping sight distance for the speed, such as 305 ft at 40 mph; add more on a downgrade.
- Stand off the travel lane with an escape route, with a Flagger Ahead sign before you.
- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: sign spacing and the taper setup?
q: Where should the flagger stand?

Michigan's Part 9 slope table lists running soil at 18 degrees, 3 to 1 (R 408.40941, Table 1); federal OSHA's flattest slope is Type C at 1 1/2:1 (34 degrees).
- Not confirmed: the official table is an image the library couldn't open, so check Table 1 in Part 9 or ask MIOSHA.
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: What slope for running soil?

text:
Call Utah OSHA (UOSH) at (801) 530-6901 within 8 hours of any disabling, serious or significant injury (Utah Admin. Code R614-1-5(B)(1)).

- For a fatality, report within 8 hours. Federal OSHA is 1-800-321-6742.
- For an emergency, call 911 first.
q: What number do we call to report a serious injury?

text:
Michigan's MIOSHA Part 9 requires sloping per its table 1 or support for any excavation more than 5 feet deep (R 408.40941(1)); federal OSHA starts at 5 feet or more (29 CFR 1926.652).
- Under 5 feet needs protection too if the ground shows hazardous earth movement.
- Over 20 feet, a registered professional engineer must design the protective system.
- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: Michigan's table 1 slopes and shoring design rules?
q: What depth needs sloping or shoring?

text:
Montana's MDT spec requires at least 4 feet of cover, or one-half the pipe diameter if that is greater, before heavy equipment crosses a new culvert (MDT Section 603.03.4(A)).
- Backfill in layers of 6 inches loose or less, compacted per Subsection 203.03.3.
- The 4 ft is the spec minimum; check the job's own specs for anything stricter.
- Your competent person decides on site.
q: How much cover before heavy equipment crosses a new culvert?

text:
For a New Hampshire job like EVAL-1, EPA's Construction General Permit governs. The libraries I searched don't give its retention period, so I can't state it from them. From general knowledge, EPA's 2022 CGP has you keep the SWPPP and inspection reports for 3 years after coverage ends, which is after your Notice of Termination. Confirm that in Part 7 of the permit.

- The permit is the authority here: New Hampshire is one of the places where EPA issues the permit [5].
- Some owners or contracts ask for longer, so check the job specs and contract.
- Keep the inspection reports with the SWPPP and the corrective-action records until that period is over.

The libraries don't cover this yet; this is general knowledge.
q: How long do we keep the SWPPP inspection reports after the job?

text:
The entry permit must identify the space, the hazards, the controls, who is involved and how rescue is summoned (29 CFR 1910.146(f), which 1926.1204(j) points construction crews to).

1. The permit space, the purpose of the entry, and the date and authorized duration.
2. Authorized entrants, attendants, and the entry supervisor by name, with the supervisor's signature or initials.
3. Hazards of the space, isolation measures, and acceptable entry conditions.
4. Initial and periodic test results, with tester names or initials and times.
5. Rescue and emergency services and the means (numbers, equipment) to summon them.
6. Communication procedures, and the other items listed in (f)(12) onward.

- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: the items (f)(12) through (f)(15) that follow communication?
q: What has to be on a confined space entry permit?

text:
You must give pedestrians a reasonably safe, accessible path, either a temporary walkway or a detour, with advance signing before the closure (MUTCD Part 6, 6C.02).

1. Post SIDEWALK CLOSED AHEAD CROSS HERE signs at the crossing before the closure.
2. Send people across at an intersection, not mid-block.
3. Put a continuous cane-detectable barrier across the full closed sidewalk; no tape or cones.
4. Keep any temporary route accessible: 48 in wide minimum, ramps 12:1 or flatter.
5. Cover or fence the open trench next to the walkway.
6. Use a flagger where trucks or equipment cross the walkway.

- Your competent person decides on site.

Want the rest: temporary ramp, edging and passing-space dimensions?
q: We have to close the sidewalk for the trench. What do we have to do for people walking?

Yes, if the truck is over 10,001 lb and crosses state lines, its driver is under federal hours of service (49 CFR 390.5, Part 395), unless an exception applies.
- The utility service vehicle exemption (395.1(n)) fits repair and maintenance work; new water main for a developer is not confirmed, so ask North Dakota DOT enforcement.
- If it mainly hauls materials or equipment to the site within 75 air miles, the 24-hour restart applies (395.1(m)).
q: Does a utility service truck have to follow hours of service? We are putting in new water main for a developer.

Not as a normal method: EPA has not approved pipe bursting for asbestos-cement water mains, so bursting more than the threshold amount has to follow the Asbestos NESHAP (84 FR 26852).
- EPA did approve one trenchless method, close tolerance pipe slurrification, with wetting, sampling and landfill disposal.
- Get the owner's and the air agency's position in writing before bidding or starting.
